posts.body:
We have decided that all discussions about AI will be contained in this megathread. If you want to discuss AI as it pertains to game development, this is the place. All new AI threads will either be deleted or merged with this thread.
What this thread is for:
Questioning pros and cons of AI in game dev
What the future of AI in game dev should hold
News related to AI in game dev
Anything else related to AI in game dev
Key terms:
game dev, game dev, and game dev.
This is
not
a thread to request help with AI, to fix resources made with AI, or sharing AI-made resources.
All other forum rules still apply
and we
do not
allow AI-generated art and music to be shared as resources.
This is obviously a contentious topic in game dev (and elsewhere) but we believe discussion is good. However, considering how all of the other AI threads have ended, we are implementing some special rules. Read them and understand them.
Failure to follow these rules will lead to reply bans and/or warning points, if deemed necessary.
Thread Rules:
Do not continue overcooked arguments.
You may share your thoughts and opinions, disagree with others, and have reasonable discussions. Heated discussions are not inherently bad. But, if it is becoming a devolving tennis match styled argument, then disengage.
Do not come into the thread looking for a fight
. If you feel like you won't be able to keep your cool when responding, walk away.
Read before responding.
We do not need to dogpile. We do not need to repeat questions, topics, or talking points unless there is news and developments. Like if you agree with what someone said. If you feel like you
need
to repeat yourself, link to your previous comment in this thread instead of rewriting it.
Link sources whenever possible and relevant.
This is a quickly evolving landscape of topics and many people are emotionally charged about it. Be prepared to support some of your statements beyond your thoughts and feelings.
Do not post obvious rage bait.
This thread is not a sanctioned location to poop all over the place.
Do not link to AI or LLM generators.
This thread is for opinions, discussions, news, and the theoretical; not for learning how to prompt and get certain results from a certain LLM.
Insults are never allowed and will result in a reply ban and warning points.
[rmod] We actually do
not
believe that banning this topic is a good solution. Discussion = awareness and informed decision making. BUT, it does appear evident that some primarily engage with this topic in a manner designed to intentionally inflame.
If we cannot have a productive discussion, this thread will be closed and we will at minimum need to consider a moratorium on these topics until additional moderating solutions can be implemented. [/rmod]

posts.author: Starmage
posts.body:
It is not a secret that I've been using Leonardo A.I. in the past to generate images (both for concept ideas and PFPs), but having amazing artist friends around has inspired me to learn to draw myself, and my art may not be perfect. Still, it's very satisfactory finishing a piece.
Right now, I'm making a jam entry for the first time with making my own custom busts, and I'm super thankful to the artist community for inspiring me and giving me feedback when needed. And I'm excited (and kinda nervous) to share it soon! ^^
I guess, my point is, A.I. can be a fun tool, but at the end of the day, it is way more satisfying using human-made assets for your games, most especially if you learn to create them by yourself with practice and learning.
You'll see how each creator's heart and soul shine through their work.
And I appreciate all artists' journeys even more now that I decided to tackle learning it.
Preserving the humanity of game dev is beautiful.

I feel a little awkward about this but I really just wanted to make a point about AI use. AI can be helpful to a developer for small and often mundane things that come up during development and can help with little things that people normally don't want to help with.
As an example, Chat GPT helped me modify the
Equipment Variables

This is a huge help to me since I can use this plugin to make my equipment have a "default" Item Image that I can change with Attach Augments and then back to the "default" Image when I detach... It's a minor change that I wouldn't have been able to do on my own since I don't know how to script at all. Plus, this is the kind of plugin change that many [if not all] the scripters of the forum avoid.
BTW, I will NOT be redistributing the changes to this plugin...  But I will show it to a scripter if they want to check the code for any reason.
AI is a tool...  Does it have aspects that are questionable? Yes, but ultimately, at the end of the day, it's a tool that can be used or not used... It's up tot the developer to decide.

This one of my Attachment notetags:
Code:
<Augment Attach Eval: Armament>
if ($gameVariables.value(246) === 1)
    $gameVariables.setValue(247, 'Power_Gun1')
else
    $gameVariables.setValue(247, 'Power_Staff1')
    this.applyAugmentSetPictureImg(mainItem, $gameVariables.value(247), slotId, true)
end
</Augment Attach Eval: Armament>
<Augment Detach Eval: Armament>
if ($gameVariables.value(246) === 1)
    this.applyAugmentSetPictureImg(mainItem, $gameVariables.value(316), slotId, true)
else
    this.applyAugmentSetPictureImg(mainItem, $gameVariables.value(317), slotId, true)
end
</Augment Detach Eval: Armament>
$gameVariables.value(246) = Character select. The number corresponds to the number of the actor.
$gameVariables.value(247) = The new filename. It changes based on who attached the Augment.
$gameVariables.value(316) = the variable for the MC weapon "Default" filename
$gameVariables.value(317) = The variable of the Second MC weapon "Default" filename
Now I just add the Equipment Variable to the weapons and change the string to the filename for that weapon and no matter what weapon that player changes to, the weapon's image goes back to the default when they remove the augment.
I only have two MCs in my game...  and they have set weapons types they can use. So this works for me...  I don't think it would work as written for anyone else though.
I got that code from the Plugin and tried to decipher it some years ago. Here's the tread I started that helped me perfect it to this point:
Need Help with YEP_AttachAugment plugin
Maybe, someone would have helped me, but I have heard them say over and over again that changing a plugin is not something they like to help with and will actively avoid them sometimes. It was easier for me to do it this way and I learned a little something about JS scripting in the process - which would not have happened if I was to have asked and gotten the answer from the forums.

true intelligence
.

AI is
not actually doing

A person thinks conceptually, linking those points together and presenting answers. This is intelligence.
AI "thinks" linguistically, scraping data with no real understanding of what the data means - but presenting it in a way that
appears
to be conceptually valid. This is not intelligence.
I'm just not fooled by the appearence of intelligence where what is actually happening is just "guessing what the next most likely word will be".

posts.author: cthulhusquid
posts.body:
I use AI mainly for brainstorming. I get writers block a lot, so sometimes bouncing ideas off the AI is actually productive even if I have to usually edit it. I also use it for quick research relating to my games, like what fruit/veggies grow well in a desert climate, or what are the ranks of the Catholic church in an easy to understand way (I looked this up on Wikipedia beforehand and it was confusing, the AI broke it down for me much better). I see no issue using AI this way, as I use it when I legitimately get stuck or need another viewpoint.
Obviously there is much discourse around generative ones, and we all know that they use other people's work to learn. However, look at it this way: we are all basing our games or other art on "other people's work" to some extent. Like how many people rip off Final Fantasy and call it their own? How many people trace over other's drawings when learning? Not to mention the flood of clone games whenever a new gaming trend surfaces.
Stealing other's work to make money is bad, same with churning out shovelware to make a quick buck. AI or not, people are going to do it, and AI just makes it a little easier. That's why you need to decide for yourself how you want to use it and whether or not it fits with your morals.

A few thoughts, hopefully without blatant bias or negativity. And no, I don’t use AI in my game development.
#1 AI is a tool. Each person considering AI must balance the perceived value of the tool with what they know of the ethics around the tool.
#2 From personal experience, I believe that the AI that is commonly available for public use (and prone to comical issues) is not necessarily the same as the AI available for very specialized use. I say that as I see my own government agency starting down the path of researching and using AI in the realm of public safety and national security.
#3 To be completely fair, if you are going to point out the flaws with AI, it might benefit you to be open minded to what AI gets right. It is easy to find the problems while conveniently ignoring other aspects and benefits.
#4 AI does not just produce graphic abominations. I visit resources every day for fun that show just how incredible creations can be from someone who actually knows how to use the tool.
#5 There was a time when many artists would have said that photography was not art. It isn’t like painting or drawing or sculpting. Maybe some artists would still say that. But the evidence is irrefutable that photography is now treated like art. Because it is how the person uses the camera as a tool. And no, I’m not saying a camera is like AI. This example is not about the ethics of the tool. It is about how the user makes art with a tool.
#6 Again, this isn’t about the ethics, but I find it somewhat interesting how many of the arguments against using AI (lazy, better to learn the skill yourself, cheap, whatever) seem like arguments that may very well have been raised about people using RPG Maker. Right? If you really want to make games, why aren’t you learning to code and doing everything yourself. Heck, RPG Maker is marketed as an easy to use tool so anyone can make a game. And there are people out there vehemently voicing their negative opinions about anything RPG Maker. Not me. I love RPG Maker. But I did specifically buy it because it seemed like the easiest option to start learning.
#7 Another thing I find funny about another point. If we want to ban sources of information that often get things wrong or are purposefully misleading, I can think of a number of supposed news sources that would be banned. And peddling disinformation and misinformation is much more dangerous, in my opinion, than the threat currently posed by AI. Note that I didn’t name these “news” sources and I’m not making this political. If you assume you know what sources I am referencing, then you may have your own bias about that topic.
#8 There are an awful lot of unethically sourced products out there. We see reports about it all the time. Exploited labor, unethically sourced materials, etc. So ask yourself this question. Do you respond the same way to those things that you have knowledge of? If you do, great. At least you are consistent. If not, maybe ask yourself why not?
Again, I don’t use AI in my game development. Would I buy a game that used AI? Maybe. I don’t know. I don’t think I have yet, but I never really paid that much attention. If that makes you dislike me as a person, based on that one thing, I think that says more about you than me.
So, yeah. Just some things to ponder.

You have every right to feel how you feel. I am just considering your wording and your reactions to the topic. First off, I'm genuinely doing my best to keep up with the thread but there are a lot of posts, many of which are very long, so I'm sorry if I missed anything important. <3
So... a humble suggestion - just an idea, but what about limiting replies to this thread to people being allowed to post no more than once per day? That would make people consider their posts more carefully, and prevent 2 or 3 people from "going off the rails on a crazy train" with the tennis match mentioned in the rules. It might also make it easier for mods to keep up without things getting out of hand too quickly? But like I said, just an idea!! <3
Others have done a great job going over the ethical issues with AI in great detail, so rather than going over it again, I'll just say I agree but I'm focusing on other points, like the user (game dev and/or player) experience, in hopes that that might sway people not to use AI where the ethical concerns haven't.
I *still* keep repeatedly seeing the argument made for using AI being "well, of course I wouldn't use it for X but I only use it for Y." X and Y vary person by person. One person might use it for writing prompts but not artwork or final text that goes into the game, another person might use it for artwork but nothing to do with writing, whether brainstorming, composing, or final editing, etc etc etc. I think game dev, especially indie game dev, is already lonely enough and when we start to rely on AI to fill in the "gaps" it not only dampens the motivation to learn new skills (one of THE BEST years of my life was a 'sink-or-swim learn to video edit from scratch for a project' year!), but kills off any motivation to connect and form community. I've met some AMAZING people through collaborating on projects together! AI can't offer that -- and if it does, through chatbot conversations, it's empty and fake. There's a reason Barclay was being treated for his holodeck addiction (Star Trek's own sci-fi imagining of AI characters, TBH), and encouraged to form REAL friendships instead. I think it would be very sad if devs stopped teaming up with other creatives because AI is "easier" or "faster".
As a player, I turn to (a VERY select few) AAA games for a polished/dependable gaming experience. I turn to indie games for a PERSONAL CONNECTION with the dev/dev team.
AI can't offer that. "But it's only part of it!" Okay, that's how much of the human connection with your players you've just exised from the entire experience.
As a player, I engage with games, whether indie or AAA or anywhere in between, because of a love of the artform. When I'm emotionally touched by a storyline, or an emotive character artwork, etc, it feels like the author/artist/programmer/etc has reached through my screen to touch my heart. Finding out that it was generated by AI and not a human would be very disappointing and would, in fact, feel like an emotional betrayal. I'm not "pearl clutching" with this statement -- I'm literally saying that you run the risk of that strong a negative emotional reaction from your players. I doubt any dev wants their game to leave a bad taste in the players' mouths.
Why would anyone want to give up what you COULD have and exchange it for making a large chunk of potential players extremely unhappy? Who does that benefit, exactly?
As my mom always used to say, "art is the process, not the product."
Regarding the "AI is a tool" argument: Sure, so's a stencil. So's a coloring book. Would you use a coloring book page you'd colored in with crayon for your game's title screen? Yes? No? Why? Even if you would, can you see why it might be seen as cheating and/or unprofessional and turn away potential players? I'd argue a coloring book page would actually be MORE appealing to many people than an AI generated image.
BTW, as an aside on the photography example -- if I take a photo of the Mona Lisa, I can't use it as a substitute FOR the Mona Lisa. I can use it to show off my photography skills, for educational purposes, etc. I also probably would have issues with publishing a book where the front cover was a photograph I'd taken of an official drawing of a copyrighted/trademarked character.
And as for the RTP, a human made each of those assets with their own human creativity (as far as I'm aware).

I'm not really sure who's going to fight me on this, but this is more to lead the discussion on the tech side.
AI is developing, yes, particularly with voices and deepfakes since poisoning those datasets is nigh impossible with the number of public photos people have just lying around. I've yet to see a government poison their recordings or require the same of news outlets, and it doesn't sound enforceable, just a way for said news outlets to make money by selling unpoisoned data.
But for writing, research, coding, and especially the fusion of all three as a creative process? I would most certainly like to see sources on how that's improving.
Writing is most likely, with translations becoming readable with a smoldering but terribly embarrassing mess going on in the localizing scene. I don't think they're bent towards telling NEW stories, with the only people who would be putting money towards that being Hollywood.
But research and coding? Seems more like publicity stunts to me, still waiting to see who exactly stands to gain from investing capital on this, and if we're actually in for a future where executives deliberately pay for bad code to require higher spec hardware or just hack each other so nothing gets done.
AI has the power to streamline and speed up the development process, skipping portions that people may not work on. Okay, I'll assume that is actually the case. Is that the meta right now? Far as I was aware, the current problems are:
Standing out from the crowd
Developing entirely new mechanics
Writing branching stories that maintain coherence and add meaning
Clunky code and wasted resources causing programs to require 10x more storage and processing power than they actually need.
Scope Creep
I'm fairly confident that AI will not fix the above problems, and could very easily make them worse. The best exception I could draw would be Scope Creep, cutting time on the "grunt work" so your project time is devoted primarily towards the cutting edge mechanics and assets.
But setting aside the wisdom of automating a foundation that you have no assurance on quality, it's a tactic that only makes a meaningful difference for massive AAA studios. Because "cutting edge mechanics and assets" for them might involve literal months flying to other countries and researching.
Is any AI working on Enemy AI and aggro systems? For something that is literally called AI, I don't think it's being worked on. My guess is that the only AI even close to working on that is for.....missiles. For the Military. I don't think any of that is trickling down to game developers.
So all in all, the technological and economic state of AI doesn't make sense to me. There are some fringe usable, possibly even ethical, applications for creating image and voice assets, but all this seems more like crumbs falling from grander economic plays around AI. I don't think adapting to changes brought about by such sources will lead to better or even more profitable products.

@Iron_Brew
Sorry for jumping in late.
Your argument about ethics doesn't seem like ethics. More like morality.
You claim AI is unethical because data of authors has been used for training without consent. But how do you know it's not fair use? Under fair use, you may use copyright protected materials even for commercial purposes without the need for permission or attribution and thus question of ethics is moot.
Currently, there's a class action lawsuit to determine whether the stuff has been "ripped", or fair use. And there are valid arguments for both. On one hand, the tools influence the market and there's a lot of copyrighted material used for training. On the other hand, many companies don't do it for profit - their NNs are open-sourced. There isn't anything that would resemble unedited or even heavily edited originals in the program's files. And the use is without question transformative, as described by Creative commons:
Spoiler
Given all this background on fair use, how do we apply these principles to the use of copyrighted works as AI training data, such as in the Stable Diffusion/Midjourney case? To answer this question, we must first look at the facts of the case. Dr Andrés Guadamuz has a couple excellent blog posts that explain the technology involved in this case and that begin to explain why this should constitute fair use. Stability AI used a dataset called LAION to train Stable Diffusion, but this dataset does not actually contain images. Instead, it contains over 5 billion weblinks to image-text pairs. Diffusion models like Stable Diffusion and Midjourney take  these inputs, add “noise” to them, corrupting them, and then train neural networks to remove the corruption. The models then use another tool, called CLIP, to understand the relationship between the text and the associated images. Finally, they use what are called “latent spaces” to cluster together similar data. With these latent spaces, the models contain representations of what images are supposed to look like, based on the training data, and not copies of the images in their training data. Then, user focused applications collect text prompts from users to generate new images based on the training data, the language model, and the latent space.
Turning back to fair use, this method of using image-text combinations to train the AI model has an inherently transformative purpose from the original images and should support a finding of fair use. While these images were originally created for their aesthetic value, their purpose for the AI model is only as data. For the AI, these image-text pairs are only representations of how text and images relate. What the images are does not matter for the model — they are only data to teach the model about statistical relationships between elements of the images and not pieces of art. ( source:
https://creativecommons.org/2023/02/17/fair-use-training-generative-ai/
)
Click to expand...
As such, I would wait with claims on ethics until the court case is resolved.
Also, initiatives for "ethically trained" AIs have been underway since the inception of Stable diffusion and as of today, there are, albeit poor quality, GANs trained purely on CC0 and CC-BY stuff - things that do not require permission. As such, the blanket claim that AIs "rip off the original creators" is too gross of an oversimplification.
And regarding AI's intelligence...
You can't really judge AI's intelligence based on the intelligence of LLMs. LLMs are very knowledgeable about data, they just don't know how to use it well... because they haven't been programmed with any cognitive abilities.
If you want a smart AI, you'd have to either train it more, or specialize it. That's why it gets trained on games - games are simple enough to train the AI and it's training based on experience - sth neural networks and humans have in common.
If we look at chess engines, we have Stockfish and Komodo - very strong engines that evaluate a ton of positions. Then there's AlphaZero. An engine that doesn't play like an engine, but like a superhuman. Instead of bruteforcing positions, it knows where to look. And it taught itself from the ground up knowing just the rules of chess.
But I digress.

There is no "license" of training data per se. All licensing comes purely from whether you have, or don't have permission to use the data.
There are companies that use CC0 and CC-BY data to train. There are databases like that, albeit small. The license is implicit and you don't need a special one.
Some employ opt-in training. Meaning you can give explicit permission to use your stuff for training. That would then result in licensed use.
Adobe obtained the permission through very... Adobe-ish means (They basically added a clause saying "You agree to let us use the data on your Adobe Cloud for AI training" to their TOS.).
Nevertheless, there are companies out there that use datasets without express permission from authors.
And it doesn't matter if you're offering compensation (Stuttershock, DALL-E), or not... If you don't have permission, you may be infringing on people's copyright.
But that's why there is that class action lawsuit. To have clearer rules on whether training using copyrighted data is fair use, or requires a license.

We've talked about this behind the scenes, and have come to the conclusion that discussion of AI needs to be put on hold for a bit.
It's a hot button issue, and it is a situation that is rapidly evolving. And I can see why people would want to discuss it here as it could be related to game development.
But, we also are not interested in having a perpetual flame war on the forums. For the moment, we're going to ban the topic until January. We'll revisit things then.
Thanks.
